documents.unit: Emory College of Arts and Sciences (Academic Affairs and Faculty Partnerships)
documents.title: Emory College Syllabus Additions (AI statement)
documents.stance_why: The text says "It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of" AI is allowed, and only offers a sample statement for the no-AI case. The College sets no stance of its own, so delegates; no tiers are offered.
documents.summary: Emory College's syllabus additions tell instructors to state their own AI rule and offer sample language for courses that ban AI. The College sets no default itself.

units.why: The sentence assigns the AI decision to individual instructors: "It is up to the instructor to determine". That is delegation (P04), not a College-wide rule; it binds instructors at course design, so before-course, informs.
units.anchor: It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of
units.frag_start: It is up to the instructor
units.frag_end: Intelligence is allowed for any assignments.
units.policy: It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of Artificial Intelligence is allowed for any assignments.

units.why: Tells instructors the syllabus "should include a statement" on the extent of AI use. This is a syllabus-statement requirement (P09), addressed to instructors and communicated at course start.
units.anchor: syllabus should include a statement that addresses the extent to which AI use is appropriate

units.why: Says the AI statement can sit in the Honor Code statement or be "its own course policy"; this concerns how and where expectations are made explicit (P09), an optional placement.
units.anchor: This may be included as part of the Honor Code statement for

units.why: Part of the Honor Council's suggested no-AI syllabus language; "Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content" for any assignment is banned in effect, which is P19 (AI producing submitted work) rather than P22, since it covers all assignments, not only exams.
units.anchor: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course

units.policy: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course is not allowed (framed as plagiarism and an Honor Code violation).

units.why: The language states such AI use "constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code", classing it as misconduct handled under the Honor Code (P36).
units.anchor: constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code
units.frag_end: a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: Use "without permission from the instructor" is flagged as possibly "seeking unauthorized assistance"; this classes unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36). It also implies permission is needed, but the misconduct framing is the main content.
units.anchor: without permission from the instructor may also constitute seeking unauthorized assistance

units.why: "Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council" sets an enforcement route binding the instructor to report; P36 (handled by integrity process).
units.anchor: Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council.

documents.title: Considerations for Detection: Artificial Intelligence
documents.stance_why: The sheet does not permit or ban student AI use; it advises on detection ("Faculty should treat these results with caution") and refers to "unauthorized or unattributed use" decided elsewhere, so it delegates.
documents.summary: An Honor Council sheet on how to treat suspected AI-generated work: detectors are unreliable, and faculty should look at several indicators and talk to the student. It sets no AI-use rule itself.

units.why: States as fact that "Emory does not currently license an AI detection program"; a detection-limit statement closest to P39 (no reliance on detectors).
units.anchor: Emory does not currently license an AI detection program.

units.why: Notes "not a solid consensus" on detector accuracy; a statement that detectors are unreliable, which is P39.
units.anchor: There is not a solid consensus in the educational and academic integrity communities
units.policy: There is not a solid consensus in the educational and academic integrity communities about the accuracy of detection programs.

units.why: "Detection programs may produce false negatives or false positives" states unreliability of detectors (P39).
units.anchor: Detection programs may produce false negatives or false positives.

units.why: A detector result alone "would not ordinarily be sufficient" for a finding of responsibility; this limits detectors as proof (P39) and requires other indicators.
units.anchor: results of a detection program alone would not ordinarily be sufficient
units.policy: The results of a detection program alone would not ordinarily be sufficient to find a student responsible for a violation without the presence of other indicators.

units.why: Faculty using detectors "should be transparent and ask students to acknowledge in writing": disclosure of the instructor's own AI-tool use to students (P47).
units.anchor: Faculty who use AI detection programs should be transparent
units.policy: Faculty who use AI detection programs should be transparent and ask students to acknowledge in writing that their work may be submitted to these programs.

units.why: Faculty should "exclude the student's name or other personally identifiable information" when submitting; this protects personal data (P50).
units.anchor: exclude the student's name or other personally identifiable information from submission.

units.why: "Faculty should treat these results with caution" restrains reliance on detector output (P39).
units.anchor: Faculty should treat these results with caution.

units.why: Names "Hallucinations" as "one of the most obvious signs of GenAI usage"; an indicator used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: These are one of the most obvious signs of GenAI usage.

units.why: Says fabricated quotations or citations "may also be an honor code violation in and of itself", treating them as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: may also be an honor code violation in and of itself.

units.why: Lists "Direct signs that the work was generated by AI", an indicator used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: Direct signs that the work was generated by AI

units.why: Lists "Writing style that is markedly different from the student's previous work" as an indicator (P40).
units.anchor: Writing style that is markedly different from the student's previous work.

units.why: Lists writing "vastly different from the class or the expectations for undergraduates" as an indicator (P40).
units.anchor: Writing that is vastly different from the class or the expectations for undergraduates.

units.why: Lists "Advanced grammatical structures or vocabulary that is beyond the course level (for languages)" as an indicator (P40).
units.anchor: Advanced grammatical structures or vocabulary that is beyond the course level

units.why: Lists "material that is not germane to the course" as an indicator (P40).
units.anchor: Inclusion of material that is not germane to the course.

units.why: Suggests comparing work with "known GenAI output" by submitting the assignment to a GenAI program, using AI to test suspicion (P40).
units.anchor: Work that is very similar to known GenAI output.
units.policy: Work that is very similar to known GenAI output is an indicator; faculty may submit the assignment to a GenAI program and compare the results.

units.why: "Student's inability to discuss their own work" is an indicator of misuse (P40); it touches P30 but is framed as detection evidence, so P40.
units.anchor: Student's inability to discuss their own work.

units.why: The honor code "allows faculty to ask a student questions about their work" to clarify suspicion; talking with the student before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: allows faculty to ask a student questions about their work
units.policy: The honor code allows faculty to ask a student questions about their work for the purpose of clarifying a suspicion of an honor code violation.

units.why: Advocates a "holistic approach" using course context and prior work to decide on "unauthorized or unattributed use of a GenAI program"; guidance on weighing evidence (P40) rather than P36.
units.anchor: advocates for a holistic approach in determining whether an
units.frag_end: full picture for the Honor Council.
units.policy: The Emory College Honor Council advocates for a holistic approach in determining whether an assignment may violate the honor code through the unauthorized or unattributed use of a GenAI program.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) policy page
documents.stance_why: The page says "It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not" and gives language for the not-allowed case and advice for the allowed case, without setting a rule, so delegates.
documents.summary: A Learning Design page for online Emory College courses that defines generative AI, urges instructors to state their AI rule, and supplies a no-AI sample statement plus tips if AI is permitted. It leaves the decision to the instructor.

units.why: Defines generative AI as "a form of artificial intelligence that uses machine learning models to produce content"; a definition setting scope (P61).

units.why: Names "academic integrity, ethics, access, and bias" as concerns, naming harms and equity worries (P53).
units.anchor: concerns relate to academic integrity, ethics, access, and bias.

units.why: "It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not" asks instructors to put the rule in writing (P09).
units.anchor: It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted
units.policy: It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not.

units.policy: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course is not allowed (framed as plagiarism and an Honor Code violation).
